g.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in
g.title: N1 [Context] (cites=0) Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in consequential applications.

g.text: Despite their versatility, LLMs often produce hallucinations, in which the
generated information is inaccurate or fabricated and require costly
g.title: N2 [Context] (cites=0) Despite their versatility, LLMs often produce hallucinations, in which the generated information is inaccurate or fabricated and require costly retraining to integrate new knowledge.

g.text: One promising method to mitigate these problems is retrieval-augmented
g.title: N3 [Context] (cites=1) One promising method to mitigate these problems is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG, Lewis et al., 2020).

g.text: RAG adds external knowledge to prompt
RAG enhances text generation by adding information from external knowledge
sources to the prompt and has been shown to reduce hallucinations in
g.title: N4 [Context] (cites=1) RAG enhances text generation by adding information from external knowledge sources to the prompt and has been shown to reduce hallucinations in practice (Shuster et al., 2021).

g.text: Nevertheless, even when modern LLMs are used with RAG, hallucination rates
of 15% – 30% (Chen et al., 2023a) or more than one hallucination per 100
output tokens can occur (Niu et al., 2024).
g.title: N5 [Context] (cites=2) Nevertheless, even when modern LLMs are used with RAG, hallucination rates of 15% – 30% (Chen et al., 2023a) or more than one hallucination per 100 output tokens can occur (Niu et al., 2024).

g.text: models can be used to verify the…
g.title: N6 [Prior_Work] (cites=3) To prevent hallucinated output from being delivered to end-users, natural language inference (NLI) models can be used to verify the grounding of the generated output in the documents retrieved (Chen et al., 2023b; Es et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2024) before the output is relayed to the end-user: the generated response must be fully grounded in the documents, i.e., it must be logically inferrable from the documents; otherwise, it is considered ungrounded.

g.text: However, as we need to check the outputs at inference time, we
require lightweight NLI models with very low latency.
g.title: N7 [Context] (cites=0) However, as we need to check the outputs at inference time, we require lightweight NLI models with very low latency.
N8 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Some recent works such as Mini-Check (Tang et al., 2024) have developed lightweight models for NLI, e.g., based on RoBERTa (Liu, 2019).

g.text: These models have shown good performance on academic benchmarks.
g.title: N9 [Prior_Work] (cites=0) These models have shown good performance on academic benchmarks.

g.text: Lightweight NLI lags LLMs by ~20% on
However, our results indicate that their
realistic RAG inputs lags behind LLMs by
g.title: N10 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, our results indicate that their performance in verifying grounding for realistic RAG inputs lags behind LLMs by about 20% (in ROC-AUC scores).

g.text: Other recent methods use pre- and
g.title: N11 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Other recent methods use pre- and post-processesing techniques such as sentence tokenization or LLM prompting to decompose long prompts (Zha et al., 2023; Es et al., 2024) into several chunks or facts.

g.text: Each of these chunks needs to be processed
in a separate forward pass, resulting in
g.title: N12 [Limitation] (cites=0) Each of these chunks needs to be processed in a separate forward pass, resulting in high latency as well.

g.text: LLMs like GPT-4 for text entailment…
g.title: N13 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) While some studies (e.g., Manakul et al., 2023; Tang et al., 2024) have also explored directly using LLMs like GPT-4 for text entailment detection, their latency is about an order of magnitude above the lightweight models.

g.text: it hard to deploy the existing approaches
g.title: N14 [Limitation] (cites=0) Taken together, these characteristics make it hard to deploy the existing approaches in real-time industry use-cases.

g.text: The performance gap observed for realistic RAG inputs with the
lightweight models may point to a substantial domain mismatch
between the NLI datasets used to train these models and the
challenging, real-world data encountered at test time.
g.title: N15 [Limitation] (cites=0) The performance gap observed for realistic RAG inputs with the lightweight models may point to a substantial domain mismatch between the NLI datasets used to train these models and the challenging, real-world data encountered at test time.

g.text: RAG inputs: longer, subtler ungrounded info
We observe that inputs of NLI models in RAG are more challenging
as they comprise longer segments with multiple statements and
contain more subtle ungrounded information as the output is
g.title: N16 [Limitation] (cites=0) We observe that inputs of NLI models in RAG are more challenging as they comprise longer segments with multiple statements and contain more subtle ungrounded information as the output is LLM-generated.

g.text: Each RAG impl has individual input dist.
While these characteristics are common to RAG systems in general, each
implementation still has a very individual input distribution: First, inputs
may follow a specific format due to the RAG prompt template e.g., question:
g.title: N17 [Limitation] (cites=0) While these characteristics are common to RAG systems in general, each implementation still has a very individual input distribution: First, inputs may follow a specific format due to the RAG prompt template e.g., question: <question>. evidence: Passage 1 <evidence1>, Passage 2 <evidence2> .... Second, the documents are retrieved from knowledge bases from a variety of different domains, which may not be represented in training data.

g.text: models are applied to data from an
unseen domain and Hosseini et al…
g.title: N18 [Prior_Work] (cites=2) Prior work (Williams et al., 2018) confirms difficulties when NLI models are applied to data from an unseen domain and Hosseini et al. (2024) shows a generalization gap of up to 20%.

g.text: This suggests that NLI models need to be
adapted to their target domain for optimal
g.title: N19 [Limitation] (cites=0) This suggests that NLI models need to be adapted to their target domain for optimal performance.

g.text: Bridging this domain gap poses a significant challenge due to the
inherent difficulty of adapting models to unseen domains that is
further amplified by the prohibitive costs of obtaining labeled
g.title: N20 [Limitation] (cites=0) Bridging this domain gap poses a significant challenge due to the inherent difficulty of adapting models to unseen domains that is further amplified by the prohibitive costs of obtaining labeled data from the target domain.

g.text: This prevents supervised domain adaptation, e.g., through
g.title: N21 [Limitation] (cites=0) This prevents supervised domain adaptation, e.g., through fine-tuning on target domain data.

g.text: To address this issue, we propose Automatic Generative Domain
g.title: N22 [Method] (cites=0) To address this issue, we propose Automatic Generative Domain Adaptation (Auto-GDA).

g.text: Our unsupervised domain adaptation framework produces high-quality
synthetic data, which is then used to fine-tune a lightweight NLI
model, adapting it to a specific domain of RAG inputs.
g.title: N23 [Method] (cites=0) Our unsupervised domain adaptation framework produces high-quality synthetic data, which is then used to fine-tune a lightweight NLI model, adapting it to a specific domain of RAG inputs.

N24 [Prior_Work] (cites=3) While training data generation by simply prompting LLMs has been repeatedly explored in the literature (e.g., Saad-Falcon et al., 2024; Hosseini et al., 2024), data quality might be further improved through filtering and incorporating background knowledge through label-preserving data augmentation strategies, such as round-trip translation (Chen et al., 2023b).
N25 [Limitation] (cites=0) However, specifying good filters and heuristic augmentation strategies require significant manual effort.

g.text: As data augmentations can further be applied iteratively, the
space of potential samples grows exponentially, necessitating
g.title: N26 [Limitation] (cites=0) As data augmentations can further be applied iteratively, the space of potential samples grows exponentially, necessitating efficient search strategies.

g.text: During this offline training phase, less efficient teacher models
can provide additional guidance using weak labels.
g.title: N27 [Method] (cites=0) During this offline training phase, less efficient teacher models can provide additional guidance using weak labels.

g.text: Auto-GDA offers a unified way to leverage all these available
g.title: N28 [Method] (cites=0) Auto-GDA offers a unified way to leverage all these available tools.

g.text: We thus make the following contributions:
g.title: N29 [Contribution] (cites=0) We thus make the following contributions:

g.text: C1: formalize UDA with practical tools
We formalize the unsupervised domain adaptation problem
under the availability of practical tools such as data
generators, data augmentation routines, and weak
g.title: N29a [Contribution] (cites=0) We formalize the unsupervised domain adaptation problem under the availability of practical tools such as data generators, data augmentation routines, and weak teacher models.

g.text: We propose Automatic Generative Domain Adaptation
domain adaptation through synthetic data that can be
g.title: N29b [Contribution] (cites=0) We propose Automatic Generative Domain Adaptation (Auto-GDA), a principled framework for unsupervised domain adaptation through synthetic data that can be instantiated with different implementations of generation, augmentation, and weak labeling steps and which automatically selects high-quality samples.

g.text: We show that our objective corresponds to an enhanced
distribution matching objective but is highly efficient
g.title: N29c [Contribution] (cites=0) We show that our objective corresponds to an enhanced distribution matching objective but is highly efficient to optimize.

g.text: Our experiments on realistic RAG inputs highlight that
our fine-tuned models using Auto-GDA (1) often
outperform their weak teacher models (2) perform almost
as well as reference models fine-tuned with…
g.title: N29d [Contribution] (cites=0) Our experiments on realistic RAG inputs highlight that our fine-tuned models using Auto-GDA (1) often outperform their weak teacher models (2) perform almost as well as reference models fine-tuned with human-labeled data and (3) reach the level of performance exhibited by LLMs while having almost 10x lower latency. (4) Our method further outperforms more classical training-based unsupervised domain adaptation techniques.
